evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The changes in amplitude of the tail currents probably reflect a true change in overall conductance.
source: This finding matches the changes in amplitude of the tail currents, which, therefore, probably reflect a true change in overall conductance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between tail current amplitude and conductance measurements.

claim: A similar biphasic behavior has been mentioned for related or unrelated mutations affecting the intracellular domains.
source: A similar behavior has been mentioned for related (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2019) or unrelated mutations (Zhao et al., 2017) affecting the intracellular domains.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The reasons for the biphasic phenomenon have not been investigated previously.
source: However, the reasons for this phenomenon have not been investigated.
evidence: This is an assessment of the prior state of knowledge in the field.

claim: An equation that reflects two components and a transition between them (Equation 3b) accurately described the behavior of the GV of both mutants.
source: Indeed, an equation that reflects the two components and a transition between them (Equation 3b; see Materials and methods) described the behavior of the GV of both mutants accurately (Figure 2A; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fits shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A biphasic GV was observed in all N-terminal deletion mutants tested (∆2–10, ∆PASCap, and ∆eag).
source: A biphasic GV was observed in all these mutants (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Vhalf value of the first component was very similar across mutants.
source: The Vhalf value of the first component was very similar across mutants.
evidence: This is shown by the global fit results in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The second component showed different thresholds across mutants.
source: In contrast, the second component showed different thresholds.
evidence: This is shown by the global fit results in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The global fit results indicate that the first component is conserved across mutants.
source: The global fit results indicate that the first component is conserved across mutants.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the global fit analysis shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The second component occurs at progressively more depolarized potentials for increasingly larger N-terminal deletions.
source: In contrast, the second component occurs at progressively more depolarized potentials for increasingly larger N-terminal deletions and when the structure of the ring is altered through disruption of the interaction between N- and C-termini (E600R).
evidence: This is shown by the global fit results in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The second component occurs at progressively more depolarized potentials when the structure of the ring is altered through disruption of the interaction between N- and C-termini (E600R).
source: In contrast, the second component occurs at progressively more depolarized potentials for increasingly larger N-terminal deletions and when the structure of the ring is altered through disruption of the interaction between N- and C-termini (E600R).
evidence: This is shown by the global fit results in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The first gating step involves only the voltage sensor without engaging the ring and leads to a pre-open state.
source: Thus, the underlying gating events can be separated into two steps: The first gating step involves only the voltage sensor without engaging the ring and leads to a pre-open state, which is non-conducting in the WT but conducting in our mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the global fit results and the behavior of the mutants.

claim: The pre-open state is non-conducting in the WT but conducting in the mutants.
source: Thus, the underlying gating events can be separated into two steps: The first gating step involves only the voltage sensor without engaging the ring and leads to a pre-open state, which is non-conducting in the WT but conducting in our mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The second gating event operates at higher depolarizations, involves a change in the ring, and leads to an open state both in WT and in the mutants.
source: The second gating event operates at higher depolarizations, involves a change in the ring, and leads to an open state both in WT and in the mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and modeling.

claim: ∆2–10.L341Split showed a significant reduction in the first component of the biphasic GV compared to ∆2–10.
source: As predicted, compared to ∆2–10, ∆2–10.L341Split showed a significant reduction in the first component of the biphasic GV (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The coupling of the voltage sensor motion to the entry into O2 does not require a continuous S4-S5 linker.
source: This indicates that the coupling of the voltage sensor motion to the entry into O2 does not require a continuous S4-S5 linker.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of the split mutant shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Downstream of S4 (beyond position 342), there is a mechanism to convey S4 motion to the gate of the mutants.
source: The observation that, in the split, entry into O1 requires higher depolarization and appears to be less likely, suggests that downstream of S4 (beyond position 342), there is a mechanism to convey S4 motion to the gate of the mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of the split mutant.

claim: Activation of WT KV10.1 channels drastically slows down in the presence of extracellular divalent cations that bind to the voltage sensor.
source: Activation of WT KV10.1 channels (best studied for the Drosophila form eag) drastically slows down in the presence of extracellular divalent cations that bind to the voltage sensor (Silverman et al., 2000; Tang et al., 2000), for example Mg2+, Ni2+, Co2+, and Mn2+, but not Ca2+.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: The degree of deceleration of KV10.1 activation by divalent cations correlates with the ions' hydration enthalpy.
source: Strikingly, the degree of deceleration correlates with the ions' hydration enthalpy, suggesting that the ion might unbind during activation (Terlau et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Mg2+ slowed the activation of ∆eag channels at all depolarizations, affecting entry to both open states.
source: Mg2+ slowed the activation of the channel at all depolarizations, affecting entry to both open states.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mg2+ also slows the voltage sensor motion that controls access into the second open state.
source: This result suggests that Mg2+ also slows the voltage sensor motion that controls access into the second open state.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of Mg2+ on both components shown in Figure 3.

claim: The voltage dependence of activation was shifted by approximately 25 mV to more depolarized voltages in the presence of Mg2+.
source: In addition, the voltage dependence of activation was shifted by approximately 25 mV to more depolarized voltages.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The transition from the first to the second component of the GV plot seems unaffected by extracellular divalent binding.
source: Interestingly, the transition from the first to the second component of the GV plot seems unaffected by the extracellular divalent binding, which could be expected if the transition occurs in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3B and is consistent with a cytoplasmic transition.

claim: For WT, alternating between –80 and +80 mV resulted in a smaller amplitude than a constant stimulus to +80 mV.
source: For WT (Figure 4A), alternating between –80 and +80 mV resulted in a smaller amplitude than a constant stimulus to +80 mV, just as expected for a system with a single open state and a monotonic voltage dependence of activation.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4A.

claim: WT's rapid deactivation resulted in near-complete deactivation during every cycle of alternating stimuli.
source: Moreover, WT's rapid deactivation resulted in near-complete deactivation during every cycle.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In E600R, the current amplitude during activating pulses increased steadily from cycle to cycle during alternating stimuli.
source: In E600R, in contrast, the current amplitude during activating pulses increased steadily from cycle to cycle.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The current amplitude in E600R during alternating stimuli ultimately exceeds that obtained with a constant +80 mV pulse.
source: Ultimately, the current amplitude exceeds that obtained with a constant +80 mV pulse (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was no noticeable deactivation during the –80 mV episodes in E600R during alternating stimuli.
source: Because the deactivation of this mutant is much slower and occurs at more negative potentials than that of WT (see Figures 1 and 2B), there was no noticeable deactivation during the –80 mV episodes.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4A and is consistent with the slow deactivation observed in Figure 1.

claim: The tail current after the alternating stimuli in E600R had a larger amplitude than the one after a continuous pulse.
source: In addition, the tail current after the alternating stimuli had a larger amplitude than the one after a continuous pulse and decayed mostly as one component.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The tail current after the alternating stimuli in E600R decayed mostly as one component.
source: In addition, the tail current after the alternating stimuli had a larger amplitude than the one after a continuous pulse and decayed mostly as one component.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All observations are consistent with an accumulation of channels in O1 during alternating stimuli.
source: All those observations are consistent with an accumulation of channels in O1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations in Figure 4.

claim: A similar behavior to E600R was detected with ∆PASCap during alternating stimuli.
source: A similar behavior was detected with ∆PASCap (Figure 4B), albeit within a different voltage range, as could be predicted from the different voltage dependence of the transition between states (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Alternating pulses in ∆PASCap resulted in larger current amplitudes and less complex tail current as compared to a single long pulse.
source: Again, alternating pulses resulted in larger current amplitudes and less complex tail current as compared to a single long pulse (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4B.

claim: K+ current during single-channel openings in ΔPASCap typically lasted several milliseconds upon weak depolarizations.
source: In such patches, we detected K+ current during single-channel openings that typically lasted several milliseconds upon weak depolarizations but could rarely be resolved at strong depolarizations (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5A.

claim: K+ current during single-channel openings in ΔPASCap could rarely be resolved at strong depolarizations.
source: In such patches, we detected K+ current during single-channel openings that typically lasted several milliseconds upon weak depolarizations but could rarely be resolved at strong depolarizations (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Such single-channel activity was never detected in uninjected oocytes.
source: Such behavior was never detected in uninjected oocytes.
evidence: This is a control experiment confirming the specificity of the observed activity.

claim: The activity in the patches was silenced by the addition of 100 µM astemizole.
source: The activity in the patches was silenced by the addition of 100 µM astemizole (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), providing robust evidence that the activity is the result of the expression of ΔPASCap.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: At +10 mV, ΔPASCap single-channel openings lasted up to hundreds of milliseconds.
source: At +10 mV, we detected openings lasting up to hundreds of milliseconds, while the dwell times were much shorter at +40 mV.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At +40 mV, ΔPASCap single-channel dwell times were much shorter than at +10 mV.
source: At +10 mV, we detected openings lasting up to hundreds of milliseconds, while the dwell times were much shorter at +40 mV.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In some cases, openings of the two classes were observed in the same sweep, with the long openings preferentially preceding the shorter ones.
source: In some cases, openings of the two classes were observed in the same sweep, with the long openings preferentially preceding the shorter ones.
evidence: This is observed in the single-channel recordings shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Any transition from short openings to long openings (or back) always involved a longer intermediate close time.
source: Any transition from short openings to long openings (or back) always involved a longer intermediate close time, indicating that the channel travels between the two states through one or more closed states without a direct link between the two open states.
evidence: This is observed in the single-channel recordings.

claim: The channel travels between the two open states through one or more closed states without a direct link between the two open states.
source: Any transition from short openings to long openings (or back) always involved a longer intermediate close time, indicating that the channel travels between the two states through one or more closed states without a direct link between the two open states.
evidence: This is inferred from the single-channel recordings.

claim: A hallmark of KV10.1 gating is the change in activation kinetics in dependence on the pre-pulse potential reminiscent of the Cole-Moore Shift.
source: A hallmark of KV10.1 gating is the change in activation kinetics in dependence on the pre-pulse potential reminiscent of (and commonly named) the Cole-Moore Shift (Cole and Moore, 1960; Hoshi and Armstrong, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about KV10.1 gating supported by cited literature.

claim: Hyperpolarized potentials drive the channel into deep closed states, which delays and decelerates activation.
source: Hyperpolarized potentials drive the channel into deep closed states, which delays and decelerates activation (Ludwig et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: The Cole-Moore shift is well described by a model with four identical, independent transitions of the voltage sensor.
source: This is well described by a model with four identical, independent transitions of the voltage sensor (Schönherr et al., 1999) and is compromised by N-terminal deletions (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited modeling and experimental studies.

claim: The Cole-Moore shift is compromised by N-terminal deletions.
source: This is well described by a model with four identical, independent transitions of the voltage sensor (Schönherr et al., 1999) and is compromised by N-terminal deletions (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental studies.

claim: The activation kinetics showed a strong pre-pulse dependence in WT, ∆PASCap, and E600R.
source: The activation kinetics, quantified by the time to 80% of the maximum current, showed a strong pre-pulse dependence in WT, ∆PASCap, and E600R, with much larger rise times in both mutants (Figure 6B; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both mutants showed much larger rise times than WT in response to prepulse voltage changes.
source: The activation kinetics, quantified by the time to 80% of the maximum current, showed a strong pre-pulse dependence in WT, ∆PASCap, and E600R, with much larger rise times in both mutants (Figure 6B; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the mutants, not only activation kinetics but also current amplitude was substantially affected by hyperpolarizing pre-pulses.
source: In the mutants, not only activation kinetics but also current amplitude was substantially affected by hyperpolarizing pre-pulses.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: With respect to the –100 mV pre-pulse potential, the current starting from a –160 mV pre-pulse increased in ∆PASCap by a factor of 3.93±0.36.
source: With respect to the –100 mV pre-pulse potential, the current starting from a –160 mV pre-pulse increased in ∆PASCap by a factor of 3.93±0.36 and in E600R by a factor of 2.65±0.54.
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: With respect to the –100 mV pre-pulse potential, the current starting from a –160 mV pre-pulse increased in E600R by a factor of 2.65±0.54.
source: With respect to the –100 mV pre-pulse potential, the current starting from a –160 mV pre-pulse increased in ∆PASCap by a factor of 3.93±0.36 and in E600R by a factor of 2.65±0.54.
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: WT current amplitude was not significantly affected by hyperpolarizing pre-pulses.
source: In contrast, WT current amplitude was not significantly affected (Figure 6A and C; Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: The authors never detected cumulative inactivation after repeated depolarization in any mutants.
source: Still, although under some conditions, a decrease in outward current can be observed during the stimulus (see, e.g. traces of E600R in Figure 1 and traces in Figure 6), we never detected in any mutants cumulative inactivation after repeated depolarization, as depicted, e.g., in Figure 4.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental observations.

claim: Compared to a –100 mV pre-pulse, –160 mV clearly potentiated the first component of ∆PASCap and E600R biphasic IV.
source: Compared to a –100 mV pre-pulse, –160 mV clearly potentiated the first component of ∆PASCap and E600R biphasic IV (Figure 7A and B; Figure 7—source data 1; Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The mutation L322H limits access to deep closed states in WT channels.
source: The mutation L322H, located in the S4 segment, limits access to deep closed states in WT channels (Schönherr et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Both ∆PASCapL322H and E600RL322H showed drastic attenuation in the first component of the biphasic GV compared to the parental channels.
source: Both mutants showed drastic attenuation in the first component of the biphasic GV compared to the parental channels.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The tail currents of ∆PASCapL322H and E600RL322H did not show rectification.
source: The tail currents of ∆PASCapL322H and E600RL322H did not show rectification.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The tail currents of ∆PASCapL322H and E600RL322H presented homogenous kinetics at all potentials.
source: They presented homogenous kinetics at all potentials, indicating that reducing the access to deep closed states also reduces the occupancy of O1.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Reducing the access to deep closed states also reduces the occupancy of O1.
source: They presented homogenous kinetics at all potentials, indicating that reducing the access to deep closed states also reduces the occupancy of O1.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of the L322H mutants shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The available cryo-EM structures show KV10.1 in a complex with Ca2+-CaM and therefore in a non-conducting state.
source: The available cryo-EM structures show KV10.1 in a complex with Ca2+-CaM and therefore in a non-conducting state, as it is well established that binding a single Ca2+-CaM inhibits the current through WT channels (Schönherr et al., 2000; Ziechner et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited structural and functional studies.

claim: Binding a single Ca2+-CaM inhibits the current through WT channels.
source: The available cryo-EM structures show KV10.1 in a complex with Ca2+-CaM and therefore in a non-conducting state, as it is well established that binding a single Ca2+-CaM inhibits the current through WT channels (Schönherr et al., 2000; Ziechner et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: Increasing intracellular Ca2+ has been reported to potentiate ∆PASCap and E600R current amplitudes.
source: In stark contrast, increasing intracellular Ca2+ has been reported to potentiate ∆PASCap and E600R current amplitudes (Lörinczi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Ca2+-CaM binding restricts the access to the WT-like open state O2 while facilitating access to O1.
source: In the light of the results described above, this seemingly paradoxical behavior of mutants could be explained if Ca2+-CaM binding restricts the access to the WT-like open state O2 while facilitating access to O1, which gives rise to larger currents and is not visible in WT channels.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the paradoxical behavior.

claim: Ca2+-CaM binding would potentiate the first component of the biphasic IV in the mutants.
source: Therefore, we predicted that Ca2+-CaM binding would potentiate the first component of the biphasic IV in the mutants.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis.

claim: The increase in intracellular Ca2+ induced by ionomycin and thapsigargin is transient and reverts after approximately 150 s.
source: Because the increase in intracellular Ca2+ is transient and reverts after approximately 150 s (see Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and our protocols with discrete voltage pulses require a long time to complete, we used a 5 s voltage ramp from –120 to +100 mV repeated every 30 s for 300 s.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sixty seconds after ionomycin/thapsigargin application, a marked potentiation of the current amplitude was observed in ∆PASCap and E600R.
source: Sixty seconds after ionomycin/thapsigargin application, a marked potentiation of the current amplitude was observed, and the response to the ramp became linear.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The response to the ramp became linear 60 seconds after ionomycin/thapsigargin application in ∆PASCap and E600R.
source: Sixty seconds after ionomycin/thapsigargin application, a marked potentiation of the current amplitude was observed, and the response to the ramp became linear.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The current amplitude declined over the following 300 s after Ca2+ rise, and the biphasic IV characteristics partly recovered.
source: The current amplitude declined over the following 300 s, and the biphasic IV characteristics partly recovered.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The speed and extent of recovery were higher for ∆PASCap than E600R.
source: The speed and extent of recovery were higher for ∆PASCap than E600R; after 150 s, the first component recovered by 39.84 ± 6.35% for ∆PASCap and 11.84 ± 3.07% for E600R.
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: After 150 s, the first component recovered by 39.84 ± 6.35% for ∆PASCap.
source: The speed and extent of recovery were higher for ∆PASCap than E600R; after 150 s, the first component recovered by 39.84 ± 6.35% for ∆PASCap and 11.84 ± 3.07% for E600R.
evidence: This is quantified from the data.

claim: After 150 s, the first component recovered by 11.84 ± 3.07% for E600R.
source: The speed and extent of recovery were higher for ∆PASCap than E600R; after 150 s, the first component recovered by 39.84 ± 6.35% for ∆PASCap and 11.84 ± 3.07% for E600R.
evidence: This is quantified from the data.

claim: This recovery time course matches that of the changes in cytoplasmic Ca2+.
source: This recovery time course matches that of the changes in cytoplasmic Ca2+ and agrees with the results obtained by Lörinzi et al. for constant pulses (Lörinczi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and cited literature.

claim: Forcing the channels to deep closed states using Ca2+-CaM could restore access to O1 in the channels with restricted access to deep closed states ∆PASCapL322H and E600RL322H.
source: We, therefore, predicted that forcing the channels to deep closed states using Ca2+-CaM could restore access to O1 in the channels with restricted access to deep closed sates ∆PASCapL322H and E600RL322H.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis.

claim: A notable increase in current 60 s after Ca2+ rise was observed in ∆PASCapL322H and E600RL322H, limited to moderate potentials, which results in a biphasic behavior.
source: As seen in the representative traces in the upper right panels in Figure 8A and B, we observed a notable increase in current 60 s after Ca2+ rise, limited to moderate potentials, which results in a biphasic behavior resembling that of the ramps in the parental mutants in the absence of Ca2+.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: For both ∆PASCapL322H and E600RL322H, the IV returned to a linear shape after 300 s.
source: For both mutants, the IV returned to a linear shape after 300 s.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: ∆PASCapL322H exhibited faster recovery than E600RL322H.
source: Consistent with the observations for ∆PASCap and E600R, ∆PASCapL322H exhibited faster recovery than E600RL322H.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 8A and B.

claim: ∆PASCapBDN showed a GV relationship like ∆PASCap.
source: ∆PASCapBDN showed a GV relationship like ∆PASCap.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 8C.

claim: ∆PASCapBDC2 lost its biphasic behavior.
source: In contrast, ∆PASCapBDC2 lost its biphasic behavior.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 8C.

claim: E600RBDC2 showed attenuation of the first component of the GV, although not complete.
source: In the case of E600R, mutation of the C-terminal binding site (E600RBDC2) showed attenuation of the first component of the GV, although not complete.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The attenuation of the first component when binding of CaM to its C-terminal binding site is disrupted supports the hypothesis that Ca2+-CaM stabilizes O1.
source: The attenuation of the first component when binding of CaM to its C-terminal binding site is disrupted supports our hypothesis that Ca2+-CaM stabilizes O1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations in Figure 8C and D.

claim: CaM might be crucial for stabilizing O1 in ∆PASCap while less critical in E600R.
source: The significance of CaM for the mutants seems different. CaM might be crucial for stabilizing O1 in ∆PASCap while less critical in E600R.
evidence: This is inferred from the different effects of BDC2 mutations in the two mutants.

claim: The behavior of the mutants is very homogeneous among oocytes.
source: We considered this possibility, but we find it is unlikely because (i) the behavior of the mutants is very homogeneous among oocytes, in which resting Ca2+ is very variable; it can be as high as 400 nM (Busa and Nuccitelli, 1985), although ten times lower concentrations have also been reported (Parker et al., 1996) and (ii) two independent populations of channels would not explain the rectification or the voltage-dependent transitions during short repeated alternating stimuli.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Resting Ca2+ in oocytes is very variable; it can be as high as 400 nM, although ten times lower concentrations have also been reported.
source: We considered this possibility, but we find it is unlikely because (i) the behavior of the mutants is very homogeneous among oocytes, in which resting Ca2+ is very variable; it can be as high as 400 nM (Busa and Nuccitelli, 1985), although ten times lower concentrations have also been reported (Parker et al., 1996) and (ii) two independent populations of channels would not explain the rectification or the voltage-dependent transitions during short repeated alternating stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on oocyte Ca2+ levels.

claim: Two independent populations of channels would not explain the rectification or the voltage-dependent transitions during short repeated alternating stimuli.
source: We considered this possibility, but we find it is unlikely because (i) the behavior of the mutants is very homogeneous among oocytes, in which resting Ca2+ is very variable; it can be as high as 400 nM (Busa and Nuccitelli, 1985), although ten times lower concentrations have also been reported (Parker et al., 1996) and (ii) two independent populations of channels would not explain the rectification or the voltage-dependent transitions during short repeated alternating stimuli.
evidence: This is a logical argument against the two-population hypothesis.

claim: A fraction of channels bound to CaM was consistently detected already in 50 and 100 nM Ca2+.
source: Under these conditions, we could consistently detect a fraction of channels bound to CaM already in 50 and 100 nM Ca2+, which increased dramatically in 0.5 and 1 µM, compatible with previous reports, suggesting that, at basal Ca2+, only a small and variable fraction of channels are bound to CaM both in the WT and in the mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: The fraction of channels bound to CaM increased dramatically in 0.5 and 1 µM Ca2+.
source: Under these conditions, we could consistently detect a fraction of channels bound to CaM already in 50 and 100 nM Ca2+, which increased dramatically in 0.5 and 1 µM, compatible with previous reports, suggesting that, at basal Ca2+, only a small and variable fraction of channels are bound to CaM both in the WT and in the mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: At basal Ca2+, only a small and variable fraction of channels are bound to CaM both in the WT and in the mutants.
source: Under these conditions, we could consistently detect a fraction of channels bound to CaM already in 50 and 100 nM Ca2+, which increased dramatically in 0.5 and 1 µM, compatible with previous reports, suggesting that, at basal Ca2+, only a small and variable fraction of channels are bound to CaM both in the WT and in the mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the pull-down experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: The fraction of channels bound to CaM at basal Ca2+ (in the range of 4% in 100 nM) is insufficient to explain the prominent and proportionally constant first component observed in the mutants.
source: The fraction of channels bound to CaM at basal Ca2+ (in the range of 4% in 100 nM), even if only one CaM is needed per channel tetramer, is insufficient to explain the prominent and proportionally constant first component observed in the mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantification of CaM binding.

claim: The results strongly suggest that Ca2+-CaM stabilizes O1, possibly by driving the channel to deep closed states.
source: In summary, our results strongly suggest that Ca2+-CaM stabilizes O1, possibly by driving the channel to deep closed states.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: The model structure presented is not the only one found to be able to reproduce the data, but it is amongst the simplest that could.
source: It should be noted that the model structure presented here (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) is not the only one we found to be able to reproduce the data, but it is amongst the simplest that could (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling approach.

claim: The wide range of voltage protocols and the concurrent matching of depolarization and repolarization responses tightly constrains several rate ratios at different voltages and, thereby, ultimately all parameters.
source: Given the large number of model parameters (42+absolute conductance), it might be surprising that all parameters can be constrained. However, the wide range of voltage protocols and the concurrent matching of depolarization and repolarization responses tightly constrains several rate ratios at different voltages and, thereby, ultimately all parameters.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the model parameters were constrained.

claim: The model never fitted all experiments at once very well.
source: This said, the model never fitted all experiments at once very well.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the model.

claim: A global fit proved extremely hard to achieve in an automated way.
source: Consequently, a global fit proved extremely hard to achieve in an automated way, and we decided to explore the parameter space manually, based on the time constants and rate ratios we could discern from the experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling approach.

claim: The model displays biphasic activation in response to an I-V-protocol.
source: In response to an I-V-protocol (Figure 1A), the model displays biphasic activation, more clearly represented in the derived G-V curve (right, compare to Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The tail-currents in the model show a complex dependence on test-pulse voltage and time.
